learn.intro: Historians need to know when things happened, and in what order, before they can explain anything. This topic covers chronology, BC/BCE and AD/CE dates, centuries and how to spot patterns on a timeline.

sections.title: 1. Why chronology matters

blocks.p: Chronology means arranging events in the order they happened. It lets historians see which events came first, which overlapped and which could have caused others. If the order is wrong, the explanation falls apart: a cause must happen before its effect.
A period is a length of time with shared features, such as the Bronze Age. Time connectives (firstly, then, next, after, finally) help you explain a sequence clearly.

A global timeline shows that different societies developed at the same time. For example, Mansa Musa of Mali made his famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, while England was ruled by Edward II and Edward III.

evidence: A cause must happen before its effect.

sections.title: 2. BC/BCE, AD/CE and centuries

blocks.p: Many historians use a calendar counted from year 1. Dates before it are BC ("before Christ") or BCE ("before common era"). Dates after it are AD ("anno Domini") or CE ("common era"). There is no year 0.
BC/BCE dates count backwards, so 500 BCE is earlier than 100 BCE. AD/CE dates count forwards, so CE 100 is earlier than CE 500.
A century is 100 years and a millennium is 1,000 years. The century number is one more than the "hundreds": 1066 is in the 11th century, 1324 in the 14th century and 1971 in the 20th century.
Other calendars exist too. The Islamic (Hijri) calendar counts from the Hijra in 622 CE. Calendars are human inventions, so they are part of history too.

evidence: The Hijri calendar begins with the Hijra in 622 CE.

vocab.def: The arrangement of events in the order they happened.

A length of time with shared features.

"Anno Domini" / "common era": counting forward from year 1.

misconceptions.right: 1066 is in the 11th century. Add one to the hundreds.
BCE dates count backwards, so 500 BCE is earlier.
The count goes from 1 BCE straight to 1 CE.
Chronology lets you see order, overlap and possible causes. Explanations depend on it.

matching.title: Match the date to its century

evidence.q: Explain why getting the chronology wrong would damage a historian's explanation.
evidence.model: Causes must come before their effects. If events are in the wrong order, a historian might say something caused an event that actually happened afterwards, so the whole explanation would be wrong.

evidence.q: Explain how to work out the century of a date such as 1324.
evidence.model: Take the hundreds (13) and add one, so 1324 is in the 14th century.

sources.label: Source A
sources.provenance: A teacher-created timeline made for this revision task (it is not a historical source), using dates from your Year 7 lessons.
sources.text: The timeline runs from left to right. It starts at c. 3000 BCE (Bronze Age settlement at Hili) and passes 622 CE (the Hijra, start of the Hijri calendar), 1066 (Battle of Hastings, 11th century), 1324 (Mansa Musa's pilgrimage, 14th century) and ends at 1971 (formation of the UAE, 20th century). The gap between 3000 BCE and 622 CE is drawn the same size as the gap between 1324 and 1971.

questions.sources_note: Source A is described in our own words for revision practice. In the exam you will be given the source itself.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "Chronology is the most important skill a historian needs." How far do you agree?
questions.asks: Weigh chronology against other skills (evidence, inference, explaining causes) and reach a judgement.
steps: Explain why chronology matters, with an example.
Explain another skill that also matters.
Decide which matters more, using a qualifier.
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning, 9 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.

full: P: I agree to some / a large extent that…
some: P – Topic sentence with a qualifier (blue): One key reason … / To a large extent … / On the other hand …
E – Precisely selected evidence (purple), in order with time connectives (green): At the start … / Later … / Eventually … / Finally …
E – Explain with arguing connectives (red): However … / This was more important because … / In contrast …
J – Judgement: This shows that … / Overall, the most important reason was … / Therefore, I agree to a large/limited extent …
